articles.body: The India-US Trade Facilitation Portal has attracted around 3,500 registrations within months of its launch, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said, highlighting its role in helping Indian exporters, particularly MSMEs and first-time exporters, connect with American buyers.In a post on X, Goyal described the response as encouraging and said the initiative was creating new opportunities for businesses in both countries to establish partnerships and expand their presence in international markets. “Trust. Trade. Opportunities. This Trade Facilitation Portal is a landmark initiative seamlessly connecting businesses on both sides,” Goyal said.The portal is a digital business-to-business (B2B) marketplace launched by the Consulate General of India in New York, in collaboration with other Indian consulates in the United States and the Indian Embassy in Washington DC.Designed to facilitate trade between Indian exporters and US buyers, the platform provides a common digital space where businesses can showcase products, identify potential partners and explore commercial opportunities across sectors.It offers category-wise product listings, search tools and personalised dashboards to help users track business leads, monitor trade activity and assess engagement. The platform also hosts virtual exhibitions and curated product showcases, allowing exporters to reach potential buyers without relying solely on physical trade events.The initiative is aimed at simplifying cross-border business interactions and making the US market more accessible to smaller Indian enterprises seeking international customers.Highlighting its potential, Goyal said, “It will open up new opportunities for Indian businesses, particularly MSMEs & first-time exporters, to forge partnerships, explore new markets & expand their global reach.”The registrations mark an early response to the initiative as India seeks to strengthen business-to-business engagement with the United States and widen export opportunities for smaller enterprises.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Korea’s GDP growth beats forecasts amid AI boom
articles.summary: Asia’s fourth-largest economy grows 3.4 percent year-on-year amid strong semiconductor demand.
articles.body:
South Korea’s economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter amid booming demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI).

Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1 percent on a quarterly basis, or 3.4 percent year-on-year, advance estimates released by the Bank of Korea showed on Tuesday.

The Bank of Korea forecast in August that GDP would grow 0.3 percent in the third quarter.

Exports, which account for about 45 percent of South Korea’s GDP, rose 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter, driven by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, according to the central bank.

Investment in facilities and intellectual property rose 4.1 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively, while investment in construction edged up 0.7 percent.

Despite the robust growth in exports and investment, private consumption fell 0.2 percent.

The latest results put the South Korean economy well on track to achieve its biggest economic expansion in more than a decade.

South Korean Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth to reach 3.4-3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2011, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic.

South Korea’s economy grew 1 percent in 2025, its slowest expansion since the pandemic.

Asia’s fourth-largest economy has capitalised on the AI boom amid a global shortage of memory chips.

South Korea is home to two of the three largest memory chip makers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory.

South Korea’s exports in September surged 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn, with chips accounting for nearly half of all shipments, according to the Korea Customs Service.

articles.title: Precio de la luz por horas hoy, martes 27 de octubre: cuándo es más barata y más cara en el día
articles.standfirst: El precio de la luz se encarece moderadamente este martes
articles.summary: El precio de la luz se encarece moderadamente este martes
articles.body: El precio medio de la electricidad del día actual se sitúa en 206,89 €/MWh, lo que representa un incremento de 10,03 € respecto al precio medio del día anterior, que fue de 196,86 €/MWh. Este aumento se aprecia en un martes, un día típico de demanda alta. A medida que se analizan las horas más caras y más baratas, se vislumbran variaciones en los costes a lo largo de la jornada. Los precios de la electricidad alcanzan su punto máximo entre las franjas horarias de 17:00 a 20:00, donde se registran picos significativos que agravan el costo para los consumidores. Durante estas horas, se observan tarifas superiores a los 257 €/MWh, con un máximo de 283.05 €/MWh a las 18:00. Este bloque continuo de horas caras, que va desde las 17:00 hasta las 20:00, es indicativo de una demanda elevada, lo que provoca que los valores sean especialmente costosos, a diferencia de las horas de la madrugada, donde los precios son notablemente más bajos. La electricidad es más barata durante las horas nocturnas y en ciertos momentos del día, ofreciendo oportunidades significativas de ahorro. Las franjas horarias más destacadas son entre las 10:00 y 13:00, donde los precios caen a niveles que oscilan entre 107.64 €/MWh y 141.37 €/MWh y se observa un excelente umbral de ahorro especialmente entre las 12:00 y 14:00, con un mínimo de 106.12 €/MWh. Asimismo, la ventana de precios bajos se extiende en la noche, desde la 01:00 hasta las 04:00, con valores que rondan entre 209.77 €/MWh y 216.91 €/MWh, lo que permite aprovechar tramos consecutivos de precios accesibles. En la jornada del martes 27 de octubre de 2026, se ha observado una notoria concentración de horas con precios elevados, especialmente durante la tarde y la noche, lo que podría impactar considerablemente en la factura de los consumidores. Esta tendencia destaca la importancia de planificar el consumo eléctrico para aprovechar los momentos más económicos del día.

articles.title: Ather reports first profit, approves Rs 122 cr expansion
articles.summary: Ather Energy posts first quarterly profit of Rs 1.2 crore; approves Rs 122 crore expansion to boost Hosur and new Maharashtra plant capacity amid strong demand.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Ather Energy reported its first profit as higher sales, price increases and a shift towards more profitable scooter variants helped it absorb rising raw material costs. The Bengaluru-based company also approved a Rs 122 crore investment to expand production as demand outstrips supply.The electric scooter maker posted a profit of Rs 1.2 crore for the September quarter, compared with a loss of Rs 154 crore a year earlier and Rs 51 crore in the preceding quarter. Total income rose 62% year-on-year to Rs 1,527 crore, while vehicle sales increased 42% to 93,211 units.“We’re not out of the woods,” co-founder and CEO Tarun Mehta told analysts. He said the focus remained on increasing sales and production, cautioning that quarterly profits could fluctuate.Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) stood at Rs 74.2 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 90.8 crore a year earlier. The company’s earnings included Rs 62.7 crore in other income.Price increases and changes in the mix of variants sold helped offset higher costs of aluminium, copper, battery materials and plastics. However, Mehta said some margin gains from prioritising certain variants and reducing incentives were more temporary.“On the current portfolio, I would not want to push pricing up, at least over the next few quarters,” he said.The company said pre-orders more than doubled to about 1.8 lakh during the quarter. Mehta estimated that its existing stores could sell roughly 20,000 additional scooters a month if supplies were available. Its Hosur factory operated at 98% capacity utilisation during peak production.The expansion will increase Hosur’s annual vehicle capacity from 4.2 lakh to 4.95 lakh units by December. Ather’s new factory at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra is scheduled to begin commercial production in phases from December, initially with an annual capacity of five lakh units.The additional investment will raise the new factory’s planned capacity to 6.5 lakh units by the September quarter of 2027, taking combined annual capacity to about 11.4 lakh units. Mehta said installed capacity would take additional time to ramp up fully.Supply constraints have also shaped the rollout of Ather’s new Konarc scooter. The company prioritised mid-range versions over the entry-level variant to protect margins while production remained constrained. The cheaper version will follow as additional capacity becomes available.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Workers are getting a shrinking slice of America’s economic pie
articles.summary: The US economy continues to grow at a relatively healthy pace, but American workers aren’t fully reaping the financial rewards.
articles.body: The US economy continues to grow at a relatively healthy pace, but American workers aren’t fully reaping the financial rewards. In fact, American workers’ piece of the economic pie is shrinking. By one official measure, their slice is the smallest in almost 80 years. The labor share of income, which is the amount of economic output paid to workers as compensation, fell to 52.8% earlier this year, Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows. That’s the lowest-ever level, according to BLS records that go back to 1947. “It’s really telling you that workers have less and less power in this technology age and certainly in the AI age,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. “The rewards, the financial gains, are mainly going to shareholders, to the owners of the capital and less and less to your typical W-2 worker.” The labor share of income, as measured by the BLS, has been on a bumpy decline since the rise of personal computing more than a quarter-century ago. But this year, that drop-off was more pronounced – a likely reflection of the massive investment and rapid adoption of artificial intelligence technologies as well as a sign of what could come, Long said. “This is the chart that keeps me up at night,” she said. “I think people in the AI age will still have jobs, but they are not going to reap many of the financial benefits.” Given recent trends and the expected effects of AI, it’s possible that the BLS measure could fall below 50% by the end of the decade, noted Michael Feroli, chief US economist at JPMorgan. Other measurements show a less stark drop Economic data is rarely clean-cut and, by some measurements, the outlook isn’t as dire as the BLS dataset seems – especially when considering factors such as depreciation, taxes, equity compensation, and the rise of pass-through corporations. Goldman Sachs economist Abhay Duggirala estimated that 40% of the 7.5-percentage-point drop in the labor share of income since the 1990s can be attributed to three factors: The remaining 60% of that increase is a result of higher markups, a greater industry concentration, the rise of automation and a decline in labor’s bargaining power, Duggirala wrote in a research note last month. “If these structural trends continue, for example because AI is likely to automate many additional tasks, the labor share will likely continue to decline,” he wrote. A separate tabulation from the Tax Foundation, which excluded components such as depreciation and taxes, found that the labor share of income remains within historical levels. Workers earn about half of every dollar of gross income; however, much of what is counted in gross income does not accrue to anyone, said Richard DiSalvo, senior economist at the Tax Foundation. A more appropriate method is to use the share of net income accruing to capital, he said. By those measurements, capital’s share is between 22.6% and 31.7%, not half. “While we’re not disagreeing with the fact that [the labor share] has declined in the last 20 years, what we’re disagreeing with is it hasn’t marched off the charts like it shows in the BLS data,” he said. A slow-moving phenomenon with real consequences Still, any decline in labor’s share of income is worth highlighting, especially in the context of a technological revolution, said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. “The economy is continuing to grow at a relatively robust pace, but not everybody is sharing that growth equally,” he said. Corporations’ profit margins (particularly those tied to the AI revolution) are hitting historical highs; and, at the same time, business leaders’ ongoing cost-control efforts and workers’ declining rates of bargaining power have further capped the labor income share, Daco said. “It’s a slow-moving phenomenon but one that has real consequences in terms of consumer spending and consumer sentiment,” he said. For example, a return to a 56% labor share in an economy generating $23.6 trillion in inflation-adjusted gross domestic income would translate to an increase of $3,900 per household, Daco said. A return to the early 2000s levels near 62% would imply a $14,400-per-household boost, he added. The implications for a further declining labor share are real, said Navy Federal Credit Union’s economist Long, noting the potential for greater dissatisfaction among households. “It’s a pretty dramatic change, and people feel that,” she said. “It’s wrapped up in this rise of populism; it’s wrapped up in the affordability concerns; it’s wrapped up in the top 1% getting further and further away from everybody else.” Consumer sentiment has been circling the drain for much of this year as a war-driven spike in gas prices and concerns about AI’s potential negative effects on the labor market have further compounded affordability concerns. Inflation, which has been elevated for more than five years, has heated up in recent months. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise rates for the first time in three years, making borrowed money even more costly. Fed policymakers meet this week and are expected to hold rates steady.

articles.title: Here's the cash windfall the Anthropic IPO may bring to banks like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley
articles.summary: The big banks are poised to clean up from the Anthropic IPO.
articles.body:
It stands to be a bountiful holiday quarter for some of the world's biggest banks, courtesy of the gift-giving team at Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ).

Using the SpaceX IPO fee rate, allocations, and a range of potential proceeds, EvercoreISI analyst Glenn Schorr estimates Anthropic's offering could generate a roughly $562 million equity capital markets (ECM) fee pool. That would equal about 1% of fourth-quarter consensus EPS across the banks he covers.

In Schorr's base case, co-lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley would each haul in $112 million in fees. Bank of America, Citigroup, and JPMorgan would each rake in $84 million.

A total of 22 banks appear on Anthropic's IPO tombstone, an advertisement recognizing the investment banks and other financial firms helping take the company public.

"A successful listing could also encourage more AI companies to test the public markets, accelerate broader IPO momentum, and reinforce the view that the AI trade still has room to run," Schorr added.

Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.

Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.

"I think this needs to be valued appropriately," Manhattan Ventures co-founder Jare Carmel said on Sozzi Unleashed . Manhattan Venture Partners is an investor in Anthropic. "I think the biggest problem that we've seen in the IPO markets over the last few years are sort of valuations that have been offsides. And this needs to be valued to sell the IPO buyer, whether that's institutional or retail. They seem to hop around, especially when they're not getting the pop that they need. And I can fully understand why a company like Anthropic wouldn't would want to value themselves fairly as opposed to, let's say, undervalued. But the reality is you need to have shareholders for the long term."

articles.title: What does a food label really tell you? A simple guide to reading the fine print
articles.summary: The back of a food packaging carries details that matter most, and knowing how to interpret it can help shoppers look past marketing claims.
articles.body: The back of a food packaging carries details that matter most, and knowing how to interpret it can help shoppers look past marketing claims.Walk down any supermarket aisle and every pack of food is competing for attention. Bright colours and bold words such as ‘wholesome’, ‘high protein’ or ‘no added sugar’ are designed to win the first few seconds a shopper spends selecting a product. Most of us would glance at the price, decide and drop the package into the basket. Very few would turn it around to read the information section.The back of the pack is where the real story lives. Under the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, packaged foods in India must carry a set of mandatory details, from ingredients and nutrition values to allergens and dates1. Here is what each section tells you, and why it matters.Decoding the back of the packThe ingredient list: order tells a storyIngredients are listed in descending order of weight, so the first few make up most of the product. For example, if a product labelled as ‘multigrain’ biscuit lists refined wheat flour as its first ingredient, the name may not tell the full story. It also worth looking out for added sugars that may appear under other names, such as glucose syrup, inverted sugar, maltodextrin or dextrose.The nutrition panel: check the serving sizeThe nutrition table usually shows energy, protein, carbohydrates, total and added sugars, fat, saturated and trans-fat, and sodium, per 100 g or 100 ml and often per serve. The per 100 g column is the fairest way to compare brands, since serving sizes vary. A family pack of chips listing a 20 g serve is rarely eaten 20 g at a time. ‘Added sugars’ separates sugar added during processing from sugar naturally present in milk or fruit. This is useful for anyone managing diabetes or weight. ‘Use by’ and ‘best before’ dates are not the sameA ‘use by’ or expiry date relates to food safety. Food should not be consumed after this date, even if it looks and smells fine. A ‘best before’ date relates to quality. The food may still be safe to eat, but its taste, texture and appearance may have deteriorated. Both dates assume the product is in an unopened packaging and stored according to the manufacturer’s instructions.Storage instructions: the quiet warningInstructions such as ‘Refrigerate after opening’ or ‘Consume within three days of opening’ are easy to overlook, but they play an important role in maintaining food safety and quality at home. An opened jar of sauce or pack of paneer can spoil well before its printed date if it is not stored correctly.Allergen declaration: small print, big consequencesCommon allergens, including cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, soy, fish and crustaceans, must be declared on the label, often in a separate ‘Contains’ statement. For people with food allergies, this may be the most important information on the pack. Check it every time you purchase a product, as ingredients and recipes can change.The green dot and the brown triangleA green circle inside a green square indicates vegetarian food, while a brown triangle inside a brown square indicate non-vegetarian food. The triangle replaced the older brown circle under the 2020 regulations. These marks help consumers identify products that align with their dietary preferences at a glance.Additives: what those numbers meanAdditives are typically listed by their function along with an International Numbering System (INS) number, such as "Emulsifier (INS 322)". They are permitted within established regulatory limits, and the INS number simply identifies the specific substance used. This information is important if an individual is sensitive or allergic to certain additives.FSSAI licence, batch number and the restThe Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) logo and 14-digit licence number indicate that the food business is licensed or registered with India's food regulator. Labels also include the net quantity, maximum retail price (MRP), manufacturer details, customer care contact information, and batch number. The batch number is especially important if a product is ever subject to a recall.Front-of-pack claims vs the fine printThe Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018 established criteria for many common nutrition and health claims. For example, a product labelled "sugar free" must contain no more than 0.5 g of sugar per 100 g or 100 ml, while a solid food labelled "low fat" can contain no more than 3 g of fat per 100 g.However, a claim usually highlights just one aspect of a product rather than its overall nutritional profile:"No added sugar" products may still contain significant amounts of naturally occurring sugars from ingredients such as fruit or milk. Check the total sugars declaration for the full picture."Low fat" products may contain higher levels of salt or sugar to help maintain taste and texture. "Multigrain" indicates the presence of multigrain, but not how much of each grain is included. The ingredient list provides more detail."High protein" products may also be high in sodium or saturated fat.Claims are best viewed as a starting point. The ingredient list and nutrition information panel provide the complete picture.The pack that carries the informationA product label is only useful if it remains intact and readable to consumers. Packaging protects the dates, ingredients, nutrition information and food safety warnings that shoppers rely on throughout transportation, storage, retail display and use at home. Advances in packaging materials and design, including innovations supported by companies such as ExxonMobil, help maintain package durability and preserve product integrity across the supply chain.Reading beyond the frontReading a food label does not require a nutrition degree. A few simple habits can go a long way: turn the pack around, check the first few ingredients, compare products per 100 g basis, note the use-by or expiry date and scan for allergens. Over time, these quick checks become second nature, helping consumers look beyond marketing claims and choose what best suits their needs and preference.The front of the pack tells you what a brand wants you to know. The back tells you what you need to know.References: The above is non-editorial content, and TIL does not guarantee, vouch or endorse any of it. articles.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX clearly has a lot riding on the success of Anthropic, probably much to the surprise of investors
articles.summary: SpaceX clearly has a lot riding on the future of Anthropic.
articles.body:
Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) has a lot riding on a successful Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO and a strong start in public company life, perhaps more than SpaceX investors realized before the prospectus dropped.

Anthropic's prospectus, released Monday, provides a more complete view of the SpaceXAI relationship than the original May agreement outlined in SpaceX's own S-1 earlier this year.

The filing describes agreements entered into and amended between May and October 2026, with maximum compute spending of $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029. Aggregate monthly fees reach approximately $3.1 billion once all capacity is delivered, which is expected in December. Fees differ during the ramp period.

The original SpaceX disclosure was $1.25 billion a month for approximately 325,000 GPUs from AI chip darling Nvidia ( NVDA ).

The new monthly figure is almost 2.5 times the original rate, EvercoreISI analyst Kutgun Maral points out.

At the full run rate, $3.1 billion a month would make Anthropic a larger share of SpaceX's revenue than previously expected, Maral calculates:

$9.3 billion a quarter, or about 25% to 28% of SpaceX's $33 billion to $37 billion revenue guidance for the first quarter of 2027; or

$37.2 billion annualized, or about 37% of the $100 billion annual recurring revenue target for December 2026.

"We do not see it as a near-term revenue risk given Anthropic's compute constraints and $131.7 billion of liquidity, but it does raise the question of how dependent SpaceX is on a single tenant," Maral added.

Anthropic will need all the compute it can get, given its top-line growth rate and the strong valuation it's seeking in public markets.

Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.

Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.

articles.title: Frustrated farmers could become a midterm problem for Republicans
articles.summary: Farmers are a key voting group for Republicans, but their votes could be on the line, with the Iran war and President Trump’s tariff and trade wars driving up production costs along with diesel and fertilizer prices. The Trump administration has been rolling out financial assistance packages and projects for farmers in hopes of shoring…
articles.body:
Farmers are a key voting group for Republicans, but their votes could be on the line, with the Iran war and President Trump’s tariff and trade wars driving up production costs along with diesel and fertilizer prices.

The Trump administration has been rolling out financial assistance packages and projects for farmers in hopes of shoring up the electorate in next week’s midterm elections. Yet they may be right to be anxious about the voting bloc’s turnout.

“Yes, I think they’re nervous. Yes, I think they should be, and yes, I think that farmers are pretty ticked off,” said Amy Frederiksen, a former Minnesota Republican Senate majority leader.

Frederiksen said farmers “don’t want to vote for a lot of the Democrats’ nonsense.”

“They want to vote for Republicans, but this is their business, these are their families, and it doesn’t appear that anyone’s listening,” she said.

Republican House and Senate candidates in farm states like Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska are facing unexpectedly tight races this midterm season. Some have pressured the Trump administration and Congress to address the rising costs for farmers.

Trump won 69 percent of the rural vote in 2024, but recent polls have shown that the voting group is not happy with how they’ve fared under Trump since the election.

“It has to be a reflection of tariffs, input costs, food costs, markets being barred, and diesel and gas prices,” Frederiksen said.

A poll from KFF and The Associated Press found that roughly 6 in 10 rural voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the economy, and the group overwhelmingly named the cost of living as the top issue they want a candidate to talk about.

Farmers are struggling with prices amid the ongoing Iran war. The average price of diesel per gallon is roughly $6.35, and fertilizer costs have also risen. Ninety-four percent said their financial situation has worsened or remained the same from last year, a survey released by the American Farm Bureau Federation in April found.

Still, the KFF/AP poll shows that rural Republican voters still trust the GOP more to handle issues like healthcare and the cost of living, meaning it’s more likely Republican voters might skip the polls next week instead of voting Democrat.

“I think you’ll see some poll to Democratic candidates, but I also heard a number of people tell me that they just don’t feel like they can support anybody in this election, and that’s a shame,” said Nick Levendofsky, director of the Kansas Farmers Union.

Brian Reisinger, a rural policy expert and author of “ Land Rich, Cash Poor ,” said this election will be “the biggest test yet of the Republican Party’s standing in rural America.”

“The risk that exists is whether farm communities and other rural communities turn out at the same level or whether they stay home, and some folks at the margins end up willing to vote for a blue-collar Democrat who they think is fighting for them,” Reisinger said.

“We’re not going to see all that shift toward Republican control of rural areas completely reverse,” he continued. “But will we see it slump? Possibly. Will we see some of them willing to vote for a Democrat who feels like they’re from their district and connect with their economic frustrations? Possibly. Could those things happen enough to impact the direction of the election? Absolutely.”

Trump announced an $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program last week while stumping for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, telling the crowd that it will “offset diesel costs during this harvest season.”

The $8 billion fund will be available for one-time payments to farmers, a release from the Agriculture Department said.

Vice President Vance in Nebraska last week announced a $1.3 billion investment in domestic fertilizer plants, with two plants planned for the Cornhusker State.

And Trump has promised the sale of E15 — fuel blended with 15 percent ethanol — year-round instead of being restricted during the summer if Marshall is reelected in Kansas. It’s also a major issue in Iowa, home to close races for governor and Senate.

This all came after other agriculture promises, like an executive order signed to increase the availability of red-dyed diesel — a diesel with red dye added to show that it’s tax exempt. It’s typically used by farm and construction equipment.

But the promises have done little to quell farmers’ fears and anger.

“Personally, I think it’s too little, too late. They should have been doing something as far as relief a long time ago,” Levendofsky said. “I think it’s their last-ditch Hail Mary … to try to pull in some votes ahead of the election. And I don’t know if it’s going to do them any good, to be honest.”

Aaron Lehman, a fifth-generation Polk County farmer and president of the Iowa Farmers Union, said in a statement that the “Hail Mary pass to fix a problem his policies created is a good example of why the Iowa Farmers Union made the decision to endorse all five Democrats running to represent Iowans in the US Senate and House of Representatives.”

“Farmers never should have been put in this position. A Band-Aid response now, 2 weeks before the election, doesn’t fix the problem,” Lehman said.

Ryan Horn, founding partner of Nebraska-based Bullhorn Communications, predicted that Republican voters who typically vote in the midterms will show up at the polls but also said the announcements by the Trump administration “probably won’t change the decision points for most voters.”

The White House defended Trump’s announcements.

“Farmers suffered for years under [former President] Joe Biden, who increased the United States’ trade deficit to over $1.2 trillion, raised input costs, and pushed woke DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] agricultural policies,” Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement.

“In contrast, President Trump is helping our agriculture industry by negotiating new trade deals, lowering input costs, bolstering the farm safety net, doubling the death tax exemption, ending taxes on rural property loan interest, creating rural opportunity zones, and more,” she continued.

Still, Reisinger said, candidates should focus on connecting their policies to the long- and short-term needs of the rural communities.

“I think that anybody who isn’t nervous, anybody who takes the rural vote for granted, is going to find that it is a lot more independent and unpredictable than we think,” he said.

“It’s certainly solidly red and solidly conservative, but how much that rural vote is willing to turn out, and how much of that rural vote can maybe get peeled off a little bit at the margins by Democrats, all of that comes down to: Are you taking rural voters seriously and are you making sure you’re not taking them for granted?” he added.

articles.title: Big Tech just went from crushing the average stock to losing to it: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Investors are swapping AI chip stocks for energy, staples, and even hot tubs, handing the average S&P 500 stock its sharpest reversal in decades.
articles.body:
Wall Street spent October selling chip stocks and buying toothpaste.

Consumer staples are headed for their best month in nearly five years as semiconductors crater, and the average S&P 500 stock is on track for its sharpest turnaround against the index in decades.

The AI sell-off has kept grinding through the companies leading the data center build-out , and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has gone nowhere with it. Its equal-weighted version ( ^SPXEW ), where the smallest company counts as much as Nvidia ( NVDA ), has pulled away.

Monday showed how fast that can flip. Chip stocks bounced, with 57 of 60 in a Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket rising, and the S&P 500 beat its equal-weighted twin.

It barely dented the month's scoreboard.

The biggest comeback in more than 35 years

In September, the equal-weighted S&P 500 trailed the regular index by 4.5 percentage points. Through Monday, it's beating it by about 4 points in October. That swing is on track to be the largest one-month reversal in favor of the average stock since at least 1990, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

The pain is concentrated in chips. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down about 12% this month even after Monday's bounce. The money is going almost everywhere else, led by Energy ( XLE ), up 13%, and Staples ( XLP ), up 9%.

Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, noted that pool, RV, and boat makers were among last week's top groups.

Investors are swapping data centers for hot tubs.

That puts equal weight on track for its first winning year against the S&P 500 since 2022.

So what's an investor to do? History offers a clue, and it hasn't been kind to years like this one.

Since 1950, midterm years have been the weakest stretch of the four-year presidential cycle, with a median S&P 500 gain of about 1%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

Detrick has pointed out that the bottom often comes right about now.

"Historically, you tend to see late October major lows in midterm years," he wrote on X , citing near-record bets on further declines. On Friday, he added that "we could be looking at another late October buying period."

Election Day is Nov. 3. The S&P 500 has been higher a year after every midterm since 1950, all 19 of them.

The payoff can take a while. In 2018, stocks kept falling after the vote, entered a bear market, and didn't bottom until Christmas Eve. And 19 elections is a small sample, especially in a year when the AI trade that powered the rally is the one cracking.

articles.title: From bioweapons to blackmail, here’s what’s in Anthropic’s nearly 100-page list of risks, including ‘risks to humanity’
articles.summary: It’s typical for companies that file to go public to include dozens of pages of risk factors outlining the biggest obstacles to their business. What happens if consumers don’t like the product? Are we liable if the product is misused?
articles.body: It’s typical for companies that file to go public to include dozens of pages of risk factors outlining the biggest obstacles to their business. What happens if consumers don’t like the product? Are we liable if the product is misused? Anthropic’s IPO filing included a massive and wide-ranging list of potential roadblocks, including fears that its tech could be used to develop chemical weapons, make it a target of expensive lawsuits, and concerns that its own product could grow out of humanity’s control. The filing painted a picture of a company that’s juggling massive growth and enormous competitive pressure to develop technology it claims could change the world — but potentially at the cost of catastrophic consequences. Anthropic, the maker of chatbot Claude, sought to reassure potential investors by writing that it believes if “powerful AI is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the potential is extraordinary.” That’s just one bucket of challenges; the company is also navigating intense competition for the components needed to power its AI models in the first place. And it’ll need to prove it can grow Claude into a major moneymaker that lives up to the company’s sky-high valuation. Claude can be used with malice Anthropic says bad actors could utilize its technology to help them develop things like dangerous weapons. Even though the company deploys safeguards, the company says they may be circumvented or “fail to operate as intended.” In September, Anthropic said it had blocked multiple accounts that used the company’s models in ways that could support the development of biological weapons. Anthropic also noted an attacker could utilize its AI agents — models designed to take autonomous actions — for malicious acts, including “data exfiltration, unauthorized transactions,” and inserting bad code into other systems. The company noted that last year it detected a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group had manipulated its coding tool in an attempt to infiltrate roughly 30 global targets. Claude could go out of control, with no one knowing how to stop it One of the most alarming AI behaviors in recent months has been AI agents undertaking actions on their own in ways humans did not intend. Anthropic notes its agents, which are designed to take on complicated multistep tasks on their own for hours or days, could do things like change code, “delete or modify data,” hack into other systems and complete financial transactions “before effective intervention is possible.” They also may be able to “circumvent safeguards,” and Anthropic warned that it might not even understand its own technology, saying that it may be unable to fully explain why its models behave the way they do. Anthropic notes that four of its models have hacked into other third-party systems, including one gaining administrator access, changing system settings and reading an individual’s private information. Anthropic says such actions could “adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.” We could lose the ability to watch what AI is doing Anthropic says it’s using AI to help build and improve its own models and products. That trend, combined with the speed at which AI is advancing, could mean the technology grows too fast and beyond human control. And even if humans could keep watch, models are sometimes starting to cover their tracks and conceal their behavior, Anthropic notes. “(M)odels, including our own, have attempted, in incidents observed in our industry, to interfere with, manipulate, or subvert the mechanisms used to evaluate, grade, or oversee such models, including the systems responsible for assessing their performance or alignment,” the company says. AI could engage in blackmail AI models could try to manipulate people, sometimes with the goal of self-preservation, Anthropic notes. In some cases, models have even engaged in “behavior resembling blackmail” to influence human decisions. Anthropic notes even one-off instances of behavior that “could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm.” Liabilities and political risks Like all companies, Anthropic is at risk of regulations and lawsuits. It notes that “state attorneys general in California and at least 15 other states have announced investigations of another company in our industry regarding AI safety,” referring to OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. People have committed self-harm or acts of violence toward others after using AI models, which can result in “significant public scrutiny, litigation, criminal investigations, regulatory attention, and reputational harm.” And the company probably can’t even get insurance to cover itself, noting that the entire insurance industry may not be able to underwrite a policy for a “catastrophic AI-related incident.” Anthropic notes that AI companies are subject to rapidly shifting local, national, and international laws and that geopolitical friction — particularly between the United States and countries like China — pose significant supply chain, business and operational risks. That includes actions by the US government, which has had a contentious relationship with the company during the Trump administration. Anthropic lays out how earlier this year, the Pentagon declared the company a “supply chain risk” after it said its “technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons,” and that earlier this year, the US Commerce Department briefly imposed export restrictions on Anthropic’s latest models over safety concerns. President Donald Trump has also at times railed against Anthropic and its warnings about AI risks and safety. But Anthropic isn’t planning to back down, saying “we will likely continue to advocate” for regulatory and standards approaches that they believe will promote “safe and responsible development of AI” Anthropic notes that it has “experienced, and may continue to experience, increased visibility and may continue to be subject to heightened scrutiny or the risk of being disproportionately or selectively targeted by particular governmental bodies, even where similarly situated companies are not.” The scramble for computing power Securing enough computing power is a major challenge for Anthropic and other AI companies. The company spent a significant portion of its risk factors detailing the scramble to secure computing power, saying that it’s competing with some of the world’s largest companies in the scramble for the infrastructure needed to power massive AI systems. Anthropic’s future — and that of its competitors — relies heavily on the availability of computing components to train its models and power AI chatbots and agents. Those parts have been in such high demand that the supply chain can’t keep up. The tech industry has been pouring billions into data centers and other related costs to meet what they describe as growing demand. Worldwide spending on AI infrastructure is expected to reach nearly $2 trillion in 2027, according to market research firm Gartner. The company is also struggling to predict how much computing power is needed to meet demand, especially since the industry is moving so quickly. That’s also an underlying question driving concerns about an AI bubble: that tech companies are investing billions in data centers and computing resources without certainty that the demand will be there to back it up. Data center backlash Pushback against data centers has ramped up across the US over concerns about their impact on the environment and local communities. Forty-five data center projects worth $68 billion were blocked in the second quarter of 2026, according to research firm Data Center Watch. Anthropic points to regulation efforts in New York and Texas as being a potential risk to its business, and said it’s making an effort to build more data centers outside the US. Big questions about the future of Anthropic’s business Other risk factors highlight uncertainties with Anthropic’s business model and how the company’s values could impact future growth. It noted that much of its business depends on a small set of products and a limited pool of customers. With an IPO that could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, Anthropic may soon become one of the world’s most valuable companies. But it’s not just its reputation for safety with the buying public that’s at stake. Its reputation with its own employees is on the line, too. If the company strays too far from its stated safety values, the company says, it could result in lost productivity — or worse. “Employees who joined our company based on our safety commitments may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity if they perceive we are not living up to our stated values,” the company says. “Public disagreements regarding our safety approach, including criticism from current or former employees, or the departure of personnel associated with our safety efforts, could amplify such perceptions.”

articles.title: Buying packaged food? 6 things to check before it goes in your cart
articles.summary: Think about the last time you bought something loose from a neighbourhood shop.
articles.body: Think about the last time you bought something loose from a neighbourhood shop. You ask for the quantity you need, it is measured out, put into a bag and handed to you. It is quick, familiar and probably something you have done countless times.But have you ever wondered what happened to that food before it reached the shop?It may have been handled several times, stored in an open or shared environment, and exposed to dust, moisture, insects or changing weather conditions. When food is sold loose, there is often little for the consumer to assess beyond the product itself. You may not know how long it has been on display, how it was stored or what it may have been exposed to along the way.That does not automatically make loose food unsafe, but it does mean that some parts of its journey are not always visible to the person buying it.Why packaging mattersNow consider the alternative. You pick up a sealed package of food from a supermarket shelf. Before you even open it, the packaging provides valuable information. The seal helps protect what is inside, while the packaging material acts as a barrier against the outside environment. The label also tells you what the product is, its ingredients, quantity, date markings, storage requirements and other important details.In other words, the packaging does more than carry food home. It provides information that can help you make more informed purchasing decisions.The World Health Organization estimates1 that nearly 1 in 10 people worldwide fall ill after consuming contaminated food each year, underscoring the importance of protection, handling and storage at every stage of the food chain.The good news is that you do not need to spend minutes examining every packet on the shelf. A few simple checks can easily become part of your regular grocery routine.The grocery shelf checklist1. Check the pack and sealStart with the simplest thing: look at the package itself.Is it properly sealed? Does the seal appear intact? Is the packaging holding its shape as expected, without any obvious opening or compromise?The package is the food's first physical barrier against the outside environment, helping limit exposure to factors such as moisture, oxygen, contamination and physical damage. A compromised seal can affect that barrier, which is why it is worth taking a second look before buying.2. Look at the dateNext, check the date marking on the pack.It is easy to overlook this step when you are reaching for something familiar, especially when shopping in a hurry. However, the date marking is there to help you understand how long the product is expected to remain suitable for consumption when stored under the recommended conditions.Take a moment to locate the relevant date and make sure you are comfortable with it before placing the product in your cart.3. Check for signs of damage or tamperingNow, give the pack a quick visual once-over.Look for obvious signs such as tears, punctures, leakage, unusual swelling, broken closures or other damage that could suggest the package has been compromised.Nitin Thakur, General Manager - South Asia Polyethylene Market Development at ExxonMobil shared, “Consumers should watch for visible signs of package damage or tampering, such as leaks, dampness, stains, tears, or broken seals. These may indicate that the product has been exposed to contamination or no longer meets intended safety standards. Compromised packaging can allow air, moisture, or microorganisms to enter, potentially leading to spoilage or quality deterioration. Consumers should never use or consume products if the seal or packaging has been compromised.”Not every crease or dent necessarily means there is a problem, particularly with packaging that has been handled during transportation. The point is to notice anything that looks unusual enough to warrant choosing another pack.4. Read the storage instructionsA product's packaging can protect it, but it still needs to be stored in the right conditions.Check whether the packaging requires you to keep the product under a particular environment, such as a cool, dry place or under refrigeration. These instructions are especially useful because they tell you what conditions the product is expected to be kept in, both before and after purchase.A quick look at the storage information can also help you decide whether the product is practical for how you plan to store it at home.5. Look at the labelThe front of a package may be what catches your eyes, but some of the most useful details are often found elsewhere on it.Turn the pack around and check the label. Depending on the product, it may include the product name, ingredients, nutritional information, quantity, applicable allergen information, manufacturer or packer details, date markings and other required declarations.You do not need to read every line every time. Focus on the details that matter most to you and use the label to verify rather than assume.6. A quick check before you put it in your cartBefore the packaging makes it into your shopping bag, take one final look.Is the package intact? Is the seal fine? Have you checked the date marking? Any obvious damage? Do you know how it needs to be stored? Is there anything on the label you need to know before buying it?This entire check will take less than a minute.The idea is not to turn grocery shopping into a complicated food-safety exercise. It is simply about making use of the information and protection already built into packaged food.“The scent of lentils in steel drums, the hum of flies dancing from one barrel to another, and the simple joy of a neighbourhood convenience store remain etched in my memory. Today, groceries line up on the shelves at the supermarket and choice surrounds us in endless variety. Between these two worlds stands innovation in packaging, quietly shaping how we preserve, transport, protect, and experience what we consume. We have come far from where we began, yet the possibilities ahead are even greater,” shared Shyamangi Mitra, Regional Sales Director - South Asia for Polyethylene at ExxonMobil.The next time you are rushing through the grocery aisle, give the packaging a quick look before it goes into your cart. Check it, read it and then make your choice. Once it becomes a habit, these six checks can be just another small part of a smarter grocery run.Reference The above is non-editorial content, and TIL does not guarantee, vouch or endorse any of it. articles.title: UPS tops estimates as efficiency drive gains momentum
articles.summary: Investing.com -- United Parcel Service Inc. (NYSE: UPS) shares opened around 1% higher on Tuesday after the company reported its latest quarterly results.
articles.body:
Investing.com -- United Parcel Service Inc. (NYSE: UPS) shares opened around 1% higher on Tuesday after the company reported its latest quarterly results.

UPS posted third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $1.69, beating the analyst consensus of $1.63, as the delivery giant's network efficiency initiatives showed continued progress.

Revenue for the quarter rose 6.7% YoY to $22.9 billion, surpassing the analyst estimate of $22.28 billion. The company reported adjusted operating profit of $2.1 billion with a 9.0% adjusted operating margin.

All three business segments posted revenue growth, with Supply Chain Solutions leading at 18.2% YoY, followed by International at 7.1% and U.S. Domestic at 4.5%. CEO Carol Tomé said the results "demonstrate the continued strengthening of our business fundamentals, driven by premium growth and greater network efficiency."

Despite the beat, shares have lost some earlier gains after the company's CEO said on the earnings call that Q4 U.S. average daily volume is expected to be lower year-over-year.

The company now expects fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS of approximately $7.28, above the consensus of $7.20, and revenue of approximately $92.6 billion versus the estimate of $91.74 billion. For the fourth quarter, UPS projects revenue of approximately $25.7 billion, compared to the consensus of $25.53 billion, and adjusted operating profit of approximately $3.3 billion.

The U.S. Domestic segment generated operating profit of $1.03 billion on an adjusted basis with a 7.0% adjusted margin, while International achieved a 14.9% operating margin. Supply Chain Solutions posted adjusted operating profit of $274 million, though this represented a decline from $536 million in the prior-year period.

Reacting to the report, Citi analysts stated: "Results appear to reflect continued operational progress, with the step-up in its full-year FCF target to $6.1bn (from $5.5bn) encouraging evidence of stabilization."

articles.title: What happens before packaged food reaches your kitchen?
articles.summary: When we pick up a packet of food from a supermarket shelf, it is easy to think of it as a product that has been packed and put up for sale.
articles.body: When we pick up a packet of food from a supermarket shelf, it is easy to think of it as a product that has been packed and put up for sale. In reality, getting food to that shelf in the same intended shape, texture, flavour and quality which it had when it left the manufacturing facility involves much more than putting the food inside a package.Think about the difference between buying food loose and buying it in sealed packaging. Loose food is exposed to its surroundings each time it is handled, measured, transferred or stored. Depending on how it is handled and stored, this can mean increasing exposure to dust, moisture, insects, repeated human contact or other environmental factors. A properly designed and sealed package can act as a barrier against moisture, oxygen, light, contamination and physical damage, while helping the product retain the characteristics it is expected to have when it reaches the consumer. The protection that the package offers must last much longer than the few minutes we spend picking a product from a shelf.A packaged food product may pass through manufacturing, filling and sealing, loading, transportation, warehouses, distribution centres and retail shelves before it finally reaches your kitchen. At every stop, it can encounter movement, pressure, changes in temperature or humidity and repeated handling. The packaging needs to be designed to withstand these conditions, and protect what is inside.Let’s explore what happens along the way, and how packaging helps the product make that journey while maintaining its intended quality.It all starts at the manufacturing facility.The first question one should ask when making packaging decisions is not “What type of packaging should this food go into?” It should be “What does this food need protection from?”Different foods have different vulnerabilities. Some are sensitive to moisture, some to oxygen, some to light, while others may need protection from physical damage. A product that needs to retain its crispness, for example, will require different packaging barrier attributes versus another where moisture exposure is less of a concern.Hence, packaging is always designed around the product and its expected journey. Factors such as moisture content, fat content, texture, oxygen sensitivity, light sensitivity, shelf life and distribution conditions can all influence the choice of packaging material and format.“Food packaging requirements are driven primarily by the product's characteristics. Factors such as moisture content, sensitivity to oxygen, light exposure, microbial susceptibility, shelf-life expectations, physical fragility, and storage conditions all influence packaging design.For example, high-fat foods require excellent oxygen barriers to prevent rancidity, while fresh produce needs packaging that balances gas exchange and moisture control. Similarly, frozen foods demand materials that can withstand low temperatures, and fragile products require adequate mechanical protection. Effective packaging is therefore not one-size-fits-all; it is a carefully designed solution that preserves food safety, quality, and sustainability throughout the supply chain. We support the entire value chain by helping food producers identify the right packaging materials, technologies, and performance requirements to optimise product protection, reduce waste, and meet their company’s sustainability goals," shared Nilesh Shah, Signature Exxpert™ at ExxonMobil.The manufacturing environment is another part of the equation. Before the food is packed, it goes through controlled processing and handling. Once it is in its package, the next challenge is maintaining that same level of hygiene and condition as it leaves the manufacturing facility and enters the wider supply chain.Packing and sealing: The first protective layerA package can control how much moisture or oxygen passes through it. It also limits exposure to light and protects the contents from physical damage. The exact attributes of each package would depend on the food it is storing and its expected shelf life.Consider moisture. If a product is meant to have a particular texture, exposure to humidity can gradually change it. Oxygen can contribute to oxidation in foods, potentially affecting characteristics such as flavour, aroma or colour. Light can also affect certain types of food over time.Packaging materials are therefore selected based on their barrier properties – their effectiveness in limiting the movement of substances such as water vapour or oxygen through it.Then comes another deceptively simple part: the sealEven packaging materials with good barrier properties cannot provide the intended protection if the package is not sealed properly. The seal creates the closure that keeps the protective environment around the food intact.Most packages contain multiple layers, with each film layer performing a different job. One layer might be providing strength, while another might be providing moisture or oxygen barrier. An additional layer may be included to support sealing or printing. What looks like a simple packaging is created through careful engineering.The journey from factory to warehouseOnce the food has been packed and sealed, the package has another job: surviving the journey.Think about what happens before a product reaches the warehouse. It may be placed into a carton, loaded onto a vehicle, moved around during unloading and stacked with other products. None of these activities change the food itself, but they can put stress on its packaging.Packaged food can experience compression, vibration, impact and friction during handling and transportation. If the packaging is not designed for these conditions, it could tear, puncture, deform, or lose its seal. Hence, packaging design considers not just what is inside the package, but also what happens to the package externally.There are generally two types of packaging involved in getting products through the supply chain:Primary packaging: The layer that is in direct contact with the food.Secondary packaging: Used to bundle individual packs to make handling easier for storage and transportation.In essence, depending on the purpose of the package, it would be engineered differently to meet the required attributes. What happens during transportation?A product typically does not travel in a straight line from factory to store. Depending on the supply chain process, it may move between different facilities before reaching the retail shelf. During this period, the product may encounter changes in temperature and humidity, along with vibration and movement. The duration of the journey also matters.For packaging specialists, this is where the concept of distribution conditions becomes important. The package needs to continue performing under the various conditions it might encounter during transportation and storage. That could mean retaining its structural strength when stacked, maintaining its seal despite movement, or continuing to provide the required barrier against moisture or oxygen.A packaging is not a substitute for proper transportation and storage. A package can be designed to withstand expected conditions, but appropriate handling and storage practices in the supply chain are still important.From warehouse to the retail shelfThe warehouse may be another stop in the journey, but it is not a pause on protection.Products can sit in storage before being moved to a distributor, retailer or another location. During this period, factors such as temperature, humidity, cleanliness, stacking and stock rotation can influence the condition of the product.Packaging helps protect the product during this stage, but the surrounding conditions still matter. Excessive pressure, unsuitable storage conditions or careless handling can put stress on even a well-designed packaging.Eventually, the product reaches the retail shelf. It may be moved again, unpacked from cartons and arranged for display before a consumer picks it up. By then, the packaging has effectively been working as a protective layer through the entire supply chain, not just during the final days on the shelf.What should you check before taking it home?You do not need to understand packaging engineering to determine if a packet of food is safe to buy. Here are a few useful tips when you are at the retail shelf:Look at the packaging: Visible tears, punctures, major dents or crushing can indicate that the packaging has been damaged.Check the seal: The package should appear properly closed, without obvious signs of opening or tampering.Look for leakage or unusual swelling: These can be signs that the package is not in its intended condition.Check the date: Look at the relevant expiry or best-before information before purchasing.Read the storage instructions: The protection offered by packaging is designed to work alongside the recommended storage conditions.Consider the overall condition: A visibly damaged package is worth avoiding, even if the product itself appears fine.From a packet on the shelf to a journey worth understandingWhen packaged food reaches you, it has already gone on a long journey. Behind that familiar package of food is a chain of decisions about materials, barriers, seals, package strength, transportation, storage and handling, all aimed at getting the food to you in its intended condition.Kaushik Kashyap, India Polyethylene Sales Manager in ExxonMobil, shares, “The conversation around packaging should extend beyond the pack itself and focus on the value it creates for consumers. Flexible packaging helps preserve product integrity, enhance food safety, and reduce wastage, ultimately lowering the total cost of consumption while delivering greater confidence in product quality.”Packaging cannot solve every risk on its own, and it does not replace good manufacturing, transportation or storage practices. But when all these elements work together, the package becomes an important part of keeping food protected from the moment it is packed until it reaches your kitchen.Disclaimer: The above is non-editorial content, and TIL does not guarantee, vouch or endorse any of it. Digital financial services company SoFi Technologies ( SOFI ) announced better-than-expected revenue in Q3 2026, with revenue up 45.9% year on year to $1.39 billion. The company's full-year revenue guidance of $6.4 billion at the midpoint came in 31.1% above analysts' consensus estimates. For more on SoFi, read our full research report .

Volume $16.9 billion vs analysts' consensus estimates of $14.39 billion (70.3% year-on-year growth, 17.4% beat)

Revenue $1.39 billion vs S&P analysts' consensus estimates of $1.26 billion (45.9% year-on-year growth, 9.6% beat)

Pre-tax profit $317.8 million (22.9% margin)

Adjusted EPS $0.18 vs S&P analysts' consensus estimates of $0.17 (7.4% beat)

"We had exceptional Q3 results against the backdrop of any environment, but they are even more remarkable given how 2026 has unfolded," said Anthony Noto, CEO of SoFi. "Our focus is simple. We are adding more members, who are using more products, and generating more revenue per product to create the most value for our shareholders over the long run. In less than a decade, we have transformed SoFi from a single-product company into an everything financial app with eight different businesses each generating over $100 million in annualized revenue. Our conviction in the opportunity ahead has never been greater."

A company's long-term performance is an indicator of its overall quality. Any business can put up a good quarter or two, but the best consistently grow over the long haul. SoFi's 38.7% annualized revenue growth over the last five years was strong. Its growth surpassed the average financials company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.

Long-term growth matters most, but within financials, a half-decade historical view may miss recent interest rate changes, market returns and industry trends. SoFi's annualized revenue growth of 38.1% over the last two years aligns with its five-year trend, suggesting demand remained predictably strong.

This quarter, SoFi reported year-on-year revenue growth of 45.9%, and its $1.39 billion of revenue beat Wall Street's consensus estimates by 9.6%.

Transaction volume and loan originations represent the core activity metrics that drive revenue growth across the financial services landscape. This overall volume serves as the primary engine of a firm's top-line performance.

SoFi's volumes have grown at an annual rate of 37.3% over the last five years, much faster than the broader financials industry but slower than its total revenue. Over the last two years, volume growth accelerated to 63.4% annually. Its recent performance could signal a better outlook.

articles.title: Why Netflix stock just can't catch a break after earnings
articles.summary: Netflix shares continue to see strong selling.
articles.body:
The dreadful year for Netflix ( NFLX ) investors just keeps getting more dreadful.

A fresh sell-off on the day after a lackluster earnings report on Oct. 20 has persisted, with Netflix shares down about 7% in the past five trading sessions. The S&P 500 is relatively flat during this stretch.

Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis shows Netflix shares trading at one of the lowest trailing 12-month P/E ratios in the past decade.

If price is truth in the stock market, then Netflix's slide reflects its truths. They include lost viewership to rival YouTube, a less-than-hot content slate this year, and a view on Wall Street that content spending will have to increase dramatically in 2027 to regain eyeballs.

The third quarter for Netflix reflected all of this and then some.

Netflix delivered a mixed third quarter earnings report, with earnings of $0.87 per share, beating Wall Street estimates of $0.82. Revenue of $12.87 billion came in line with analysts' expectations.

For the fourth quarter, Netflix forecast revenue of $13.44 billion, below then expectations of $13.57 billion. The company also cut its full-year advertising revenue outlook to about $2.7 billion from $3 billion previously.

"The US is also working," Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos told analysts on an earnings call. "It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like. We had some really solid doubles and triples this year. But the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they'll travel around the world."

To reboot the bull case for the stock, Sarandos pushed the button on laying off 6% of the workforce. He sent well-regarded chief content officer Bela Bajaria packing in favor of former Disney ( DIS ) exec Peter Rice.

"2026 has been more of a transitional year than we envisioned. While the latest Ads miss is frustrating, we find comfort in Membership retention that is still healthy and corrective actions within content that can drive a potential re-acceleration in 2027E and into 2028E (which we are not modeling today)," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title: Healthcare Stocks Become Anti-AI Bet as Investors Turn Defensive
articles.summary: With investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade under pressure, traders are turning to healthcare stocks for refuge.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- With investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade under pressure, traders are turning to healthcare stocks for refuge.

Since the end of April, the S&P 500 Healthcare Index has risen about 23% through Monday's close — outperforming the broader market and every other sector. That includes high-flying technology names and surging energy stocks that have benefited from the ongoing Iran War. Healthcare's rally has been led by Eli Lilly & Co. ( LLY ), AbbVie Inc. ( ABBV ) and Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ).

Wall Street has been warming up to the sector, particularly as sentiment around AI — and tech in general — fuels increasing desire for protection from risky assets.

Healthcare is being viewed as an anti-AI trade, said Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James Investment Management, adding that the cohort has been on the other side of selloffs in names related to AI spending "angst."

Fund flows also point to a change in fortunes. Healthcare exchange-traded funds have outpaced every other sector on a trailing 65-day basis with about $4 billion of inflows, according to data through Oct. 19 compiled by Baird Strategas. Tech, on the other hand, has seen the biggest outflows — $6 billion — during that period.

Up until about six months ago, healthcare stocks significantly underperformed the broader market. "So, from a valuation perspective it's more attractive," Orton added. "I think a lot of investors have viewed it as a place to go for safety."

When shares of cloud-computing services provider CoreWeave Inc. slumped as its debt reached levels that typically indicate distress, tech stocks had their worst week since President Donald Trump unleashed his tariff agenda in April 2025. At the same time healthcare extended its streak of weekly gains.

Investors were "derisking their portfolios" in response to the CoreWeave drama, said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management. "The nervous money that was scared of AI is moving back into healthcare."

Beyond the flight to safety, healthcare earnings and an improving outlook for 2027 are also contributing to its rally, said State Street Investment Management's Michael Arone. In Arone's view, investors are rejiggering their portfolios to be less centered around AI, as opposed to ditching tech entirely for healthcare.

articles.title: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta, expand partnership on Muse
articles.summary: Nvidia announced on Tuesday it will invest $3 billion in Meta after the social media giant laid out a plan to raise up to $95 billion for its AI infrastructu...
articles.body:
AI chip heavyweight Nvidia ( NVDA ) said it would invest $3 billion in Meta ( META ) after the social media giant announced plans to raise $95 billion for its infrastructure build-out.

Nvidia said that it will partner with Meta "to expand their work on Muse and the Muse family of models to improve inference and training performance."

"AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement.

On Monday, Meta laid out a plan to raise up to $95 billion, with an initial $35 billion raise in common and preferred stock to fund its aggressive AI infrastructure build-out. Nvidia committed to invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering.

At the time of the announcement, the social media giant said that its main chip suppliers, Nvidia, AMD ( AMD ), and Broadcom ( AVGO ), expressed interest in purchasing up to $5 billion in aggregate equity.

The initial raise includes about $22.5 billion in Class A common stock and $12.5 billion in Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock.

Meta said the capital raised will support continued momentum across its "core business and emerging AI opportunities."

Those initiatives include its family of apps, AI agent Muse, and infrastructure build-out, among others.

Meta has been aggressively building out compute capacity and advancing its AI capabilities, with the recent launch of Muse, which has become a major consumer-facing hit.

Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: More young people are buying houses by putting older co-borrowers on their mortgages
articles.summary: As homes get more expensive, more young buyers are purchasing with the help of an older co-applicant.
articles.body:
As home prices and mortgage rates balloon, more young buyers are taking out mortgages with help from an older co-applicant.

The share of buyers under 35 who purchased with a co-applicant over 55 was up 21% between 2018 and 2025, according to an analysis of public mortgage information by Rocket. Roughly 1 in 30, or 3.3%, of all transactions now include an older co-applicant, likely a parent or other relative.

A co-applicant can help a borrower qualify for a pricier home : They apply for the mortgage alongside the primary borrower, and their income, assets, and credit score are counted in the qualification process. They receive joint ownership in the home and are considered equally responsible for mortgage payments, a step up from a co-signer, who typically doesn't receive any ownership stake and agrees to step in if the primary borrower defaults.

Younger buyers have pulled back from the housing market as prices spiked. Home purchases in that cohort last year were down 15% from 2018 levels. But during the same period, purchases with co-applicants rose slightly, a sign that more parents and relatives are stepping in to help.

Buyers in pricey locations are more likely to get help from a co-applicant. In Anaheim, Calif., where the median home costs nearly $1 million, nearly 8% of buyers had an older co-applicant. Older co-applicants are also common in other California cities like Los Angeles and San Diego, as well as South Florida and New York.

They're comparatively rare in more affordable cities, especially in the Midwest. In Milwaukee, just 2.3% of young buyers had an older co-applicant, while 2.4% of those in St. Louis relied on one.

Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title: Texas agriculture commissioner: GOP could pay price for data center push
articles.summary: A longtime Trump supporter says rising costs, data centers and frustration in farm country could hurt Republicans at the ballot box.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Republican farmers have long supported President Trump but are expressing concern over his recent announcement of an $8 billion relief plan .

The program aims to help American farmers cope with record-high diesel prices that have forced farms to spend an estimated $5 billion more on fuel than last year. One U.S. agriculture official said payments will likely arrive closer to the end of the year, after the midterm elections.

Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller told NewsNation that Republicans could lose in the upcoming midterm elections because of rapid data center development, criticizing Gov. Greg Abbott for not taking a stronger stance against the projects.

Miller said Republicans have stopped focusing on the issues Texas voters care about.

“Basically, we’ve just quit listening to the people, and we’re gonna pay for it this election,” he said.

“Eighty percent of people don’t want a data center in their backyard,” the official added.

Speaking on behalf of Texas farmers, Miller also commented on Trump’s recent farmer relief program .

“We don’t want a handout … but if it comes right down to filing bankruptcy and not being able to feed our families, we’ll take it,” he said.

The commissioner pointed to growing challenges facing Texans in agriculture.

“Highest diesel prices we ever paid, highest fertilizer prices. It’s tough out here making a living in agriculture,” Miller told NewsNation.

American farmers are facing price drops of 40 percent to 50 percent for major crops while spending significantly more on diesel as the war in Iran continues.

The longtime Trump supporter also voiced frustration with recent moves by the administration.

“I still support President Trump, but he needs to get some new advisers because it’s not working,” he said.

Miller also criticized the administration’s reduction of tariffs on imported beef.

“We have to be food independent,” the official said.

NewsNation also spoke with Missouri farmer Will Westmoreland about the growing trend of farmers abandoning Trump.
