articles.title: SoFi stock jumps as consumer lending boom kicks into higher gear
articles.summary: SoFi Technologies reported better-than-expected third quarter revenue and profit as its lending engine roared.
articles.body:
Shares of SoFi Technologies Inc. ( SOFI ) jumped more than 11% in early trading on Tuesday after the fintech bank reported better-than-expected third quarter revenue and profit as its lending engine roared.

The San Francisco-based lending and investing app reported net income rose 73% to $241 million, or $0.18 in adjusted earnings per share, while revenue climbed 43% to $1.38 billion. Both figures outpaced analyst expectations of $1.27 billion and $226 million.

"These are strong results in any environment, but they're even more remarkable when considering how 2026 has turned out," CEO Anthony Noto said at the beginning of SoFi's call with analysts.

The company also raised its adjusted revenue for the full year to $5 billion from a range of $4.75 billion to $4.85 billion and upped its forecast for annual earnings per share by one cent to $0.61.

SoFi's stock rose more than 10% early Tuesday, putting it on pace for its best day in twelve weeks, according to Yahoo Finance's tally. The rally brings relief for shareholders who have seen the value in their holdings drop 50% from its peak a year ago through its Monday closing price.

2026 hasn't been an easy year for the fintech bank. Along with a short seller attack , the company has faced valuation concerns amid its move to take more balance sheet risk by growing its core lending business as borrowing costs have climbed.

During Tuesday's earnings call, CEO Noto said the company is thriving despite borrowing costs rising more than management initially expected at the beginning of the year. He also took aim at the company's critics.

"Leading our team is a privilege, especially this year as we've methodically delivered results that directly refute many of the prognostications of the haters," he said.

SoFi's lending engine drove the upbeat results. Adjusted revenue from SoFi's lending business was $807 million, far exceeding analyst expectations of $711 million.

The bank's total loan originations jumped 71% from a year ago to a record $16.9 billion. Personal loan originations jumped 69% to $12.6 billion. Student loan originations nearly doubled to $2.9 billion, while home loan originations rose 44% to $1.36 billion.

Lending revenue accounted for 59% of SoFi's total adjusted net revenue, up from 51% a year ago.

Credit quality remained stable despite rising borrowing costs in the quarter. The bank's annualized charge-off rate for personal loans fell to 2.26% from 2.62% in the previous quarter.

"We are not seeing evidence of a slowdown in how many members borrow, spend… save, or invest," Noto added.

articles.title: Meta's nearly $100 billion stock sale is a turning point for how Big Tech pays for AI
articles.summary: For a decade, Big Tech's cash machines paid for every moonshot. Now Meta is passing the hat to shareholders.
articles.body:
For a decade, Big Tech's cash machines paid for every moonshot. Now Meta ( META ) is passing the hat, and the plan behind it began with a standoff between Mark Zuckerberg and his board.

Meta is selling nearly $100 billion of stock to pay for AI . Even Nvidia ( NVDA ) is chipping in $3 billion. The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying its stock, too.

Meta isn't the only giant coming up short. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) each spent more than their businesses brought in during a quarter this year, then borrowed heavily. Meta is the first to hand much of the bill to shareholders instead.

Meta priced $25 billion of regular stock at $625 a share, below Friday's close. Another $12.5 billion went into preferred stock that pays 6.5% and turns into common stock in 2029.

The biggest piece, up to $60 billion, hasn't been sold yet. It's a new class of nonvoting stock that Meta plans to sell a little at a time starting next year.

Last quarter, Meta spent almost $34 billion on buildings and equipment, mostly for AI. Its business brought in almost $33 billion of cash. That pushed free cash flow negative for the first time since 2012, the year Meta went public.

The company that bought back about $45 billion of its own stock in 2021 hasn't bought back a share in a year. Now it's selling.

A house, a board and a stock with no vote

Meta's nonvoting shares grew out of a fight over Zuckerberg's taxes, a company filing shows . He told the board he planned to leave California before the Nov. 3 vote on a billionaire tax. At a Sept. 9 board dinner, he said he'd list his Palo Alto home within days.

Five days later, they struck a deal. Every shareholder gets a free nonvoting share for each share owned, the same kind Meta plans to sell . The filing says Meta needs to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years.

Zuckerberg owns about 13% of Meta but controls about 61% of the votes, and shares without a vote keep it that way. Your money is welcome. Your vote isn't needed.

The cost of insuring Meta's debt against default hit a record 127 basis points Friday, then eased Monday even as the stock slipped. At 120, Meta's five-year credit default swaps imply nearly a 10% chance of default over five years, up from about 4% a year ago, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Bond investors are more worried than stock investors. The riskiest junk bonds now pay nearly 8 percentage points more than slightly safer ones, according to BTIG data cited by The Market Ear . The last four times the gap got that wide, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was already down at least 12% from its high. Today it's only about 2% off.

articles.title: Gas prices under Trump 2.0 are now higher on average than during Biden's 4 years in office
articles.summary: New data shows that gas prices since Jan. 20, 2025 have averaged $3.458 per gallon, the first time in President Trump's second term that the average has surp...
articles.body:
New data from the Energy Information Administration showed that gas prices since Jan. 20, 2025 have averaged $3.458 per gallon — the first time in President Trump's second term that overall average gas prices have surpassed the average seen during President Biden's four years in office.

The weekly government data, released Tuesday, shows a reading of $4.269 per gallon for Oct. 26, which nudged up the average price under Trump — from Jan. 27, 2025 to this week. It has now surpassed the $3.455-per-gallon average seen from Jan. 25, 2021, to Jan. 20, 2025.

Trump's gas price record is narrowly favorable to Biden's when comparing the first 91 weekly readings of both men's presidencies. "US Regular Gasoline Prices" from Jan. 25, 2021 to Oct. 24, 2022 averaged $3.517 per gallon.

Biden oversaw a spike in prices — including the highest gas prices on record of $5.006 per gallon the week of June 13, 2022 — as the US confronted oil shocks that followed Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The new numbers come exactly one week before the midterm elections and underline a clear political challenge for Trump and his party as polling shows that voters blame the president for gas price increases , which spiked immediately following the invasion of Iran earlier this year.

The gas price data also cuts against the president's message, which has been a consistent promise since the 2024 campaign to lower energy prices through new drilling.

Just this past weekend at a rally in Georgia , Trump offered his oft-repeated message that high gas prices are worth it, describing them as "temporarily high."

"You're still paying lower than Biden or Obama," he said.

Yet gas prices in Trump's second term are now essentially equal to Biden's and are significantly higher than the $2.476 per gallon average seen during Trump's first term as well as the $2.969 per gallon average during President Obama's eight years in office, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis of the EIA data.

At the Georgia rally, Trump celebrated another effect of high gas prices: bigger oil company profits.

"Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East," the president said, citing increased exports of US oil at higher prices.

He added that his advisers urged him not to make that point and acknowledged that bad headlines could follow, "but I said, 'I don't give a damn, I'm going to say it: We are making a freaking fortune.'"

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.
